lesson.title: Undoing a Function: The Search for f Inverse
lesson.summary: This section defines the inverse of a function as the rule that reverses its input output pairing, explains when an inverse exists, and walks through finding one algebraically.
lesson.body:
Every function pairs each input with exactly one output, but sometimes you want to run that process backward: given the output, recover the input that produced it. The function that does this reversal, when it exists, is called the inverse of f and is written f^-1. Note that the -1 here is not an exponent, f^-1(x) does not mean 1/f(x). Instead, f^-1 is defined by the property that it undoes f completely: f(f^-1(x)) = x for every x in the domain of f^-1, and f^-1(f(x)) = x for every x in the domain of f. Composition, an operation already familiar from the previous section, is exactly the tool used to state and check this relationship.

Not every function has an inverse. Because a function can only output one value that maps back to a given input, f needs to be one to one: no two different inputs can produce the same output. Graphically this is the horizontal line test, if any horizontal line crosses the graph more than once, the function is not one to one and no inverse function exists over the whole domain. Domain and range become critical here, because restricting the domain of a function can turn a non-invertible function into an invertible one, and swapping domain and range is precisely what happens when you form an inverse: the domain of f^-1 equals the range of f, and the range of f^-1 equals the domain of f.

To find an inverse algebraically, write y = f(x), swap the roles of x and y, and solve for the new y. Consider f(x) = 3x - 5. Setting y = 3x - 5 and swapping gives x = 3y - 5. Solving for y: x + 5 = 3y, so y = (x+5)/3. Therefore f^-1(x) = (x+5)/3.

Always verify an inverse by composing. Check f(f^-1(x)): substitute (x+5)/3 into f, giving 3 * ((x+5)/3) - 5 = (x+5) - 5 = x, exactly as required. Check the other direction too, f^-1(f(x)): substitute 3x-5 into f^-1, giving ((3x-5)+5)/3 = 3x/3 = x. Both compositions collapse to x, confirming the inverse is correct.

For a function that is not naturally one to one, restricting the domain rescues invertibility. Take f(x) = x^2, which fails the horizontal line test over all real numbers since both x = 2 and x = -2 produce f(x) = 4. But if the domain is restricted to x >= 0, the function becomes one to one, with range y >= 0. Its inverse is f^-1(x) = sqrt(x), whose domain is x >= 0 and whose range is y >= 0, exactly the domain and range of f with the roles swapped. This is why square root functions are typically only defined for nonnegative inputs, they are built to be inverses of a domain-restricted squaring function.
